entries.note: A word in another language that looks or sounds like one you know but means something else; some are also [[see:false cognate]]s, many are true [[see:cognate]]s.
A [[see:false friend]] whose resemblance is coincidental because the words come from completely different sources.
Linguists' term for a word sharing a common source with another, like English and French [[see:magazine]].
Originally a storehouse, then a store for bullets or for gathered articles; [[see:The Gentleman's Magazine]] was the first periodical so called; cognate of French [[same-root:magazine (French)]].
French for a shop, from the same storehouse word as English [[same-root:magazine]].
The first periodical called a [[see:magazine]], a name meant to sound manly.
In English, understanding someone's feelings at an emotional level, unlike its modern Greek counterpart [[same-root:εμπάθεια]].
Modern Greek for malice or strong prejudice, built like English [[same-root:empathy]] from 'in' plus [[from:pathos]], feeling.
French for simply nice, sharing a source with the more specific English [[same-root:sympathetic]].
German for simply nice, sharing a source with the more specific English [[same-root:sympathetic]].
In English a much more specific way of being nice than French [[same-root:sympathique]] or German [[same-root:sympathisch]].
In English a glitzy gambling venue, much narrower than the Italian [[see:casino (Italian)]].
Italian word that can mean a brothel, a mess, a noisy situation or a large amount of something, far broader than English [[see:casino]].
In English just a head cook, though French [[from:chef (French)]] means any boss.
French for a boss, so a kitchen's head is a [[see:chef de cuisine]]; English borrowed it earlier as [[gave:chief]].
An earlier borrowing of French [[from:chef (French)]], meaning boss.
French for the head of a kitchen, needed because French [[see:chef (French)]] alone just means boss.
French for sensitive, and the source of English [[gave:sensible]]; the French for sensible is [[see:raisonnable]].
From French [[from:sensible (French)]], which means sensitive rather than sensible.
What French uses to mean sensible; also the source of English [[gave:reasonable]].
From French [[from:raisonnable]].
In French, to have caractère is to have a terrible temper, from the idea of distinctive behaviour.
Borrowed from French [[from:demander]], simply to ask, but narrowed to asking with force because English already had ask.
French for simply to ask, the source of English [[gave:demand]].
French for ordering food, without literally commanding the server; English [[see:order]] works similarly.
Jess notes English also orders food, which elsewhere could sound like giving orders, as with French [[see:commander]].
Its sense of cheating is truer to Latin and Old French than modern French [[same-root:décevoir]], to disappoint: English more French than French.
Modern French for to disappoint, from unmet expectations leaving you feeling deceived; English [[same-root:deceive]] keeps the older meaning.
Paired with French [[same-root:recevoir]] to show how English -ceive matches French -cevoir, as with [[see:deceive]].
French counterpart of [[same-root:receive]], showing the pattern behind [[see:décevoir]].
Paired with French [[same-root:concevoir]] to show how English -ceive matches French -cevoir, as with [[see:deceive]].
French counterpart of [[same-root:conceive]], showing the pattern behind [[see:décevoir]].
From a root meaning to attack, strive after or beg; once immodest or saucy, it pejorated to irritable while French [[same-root:pétulant (French)]] ameliorated.
French for playful, an ameliorated sense, whereas English [[same-root:petulant]] came to mean irritable.
German for poison, from the same source as English [[same-root:gift]]: something given, pleasant or not.
Swedish for poison, like German [[same-root:Gift (German)]], and also for married.
Simply something that has been given, like a present; shares its source with German [[same-root:Gift (German)]], poison.
A variant of [[same-root:travail]] from French [[from:travailler]], to work, so it implies a rough journey.
French for to work, not to move around; the source of English [[gave:travel]] and [[gave:travail]].
Also from French [[from:travailler]]; an [[see:etymological doublet]] of [[same-root:travel]].
Based on the French word for day, [[from:jour]], so it implies a day's travel.
French for day, not travel of any sort, though English [[gave:journey]] is based on it.
Words from the same source that ended up with different meanings, like [[see:travail]] and [[see:travel]].
French for to stay, not to rest; English [[unrelated:rest]] meaning repose isn't from it, but [[gave:the rest]] is.
In the sense of repose, Germanic through and through, not from French [[unrelated:rester]] as Rob assumed.
Itself a French word; the French for to rest is [[see:repos]].
Given as the French for to rest, related to English [[see:repose]].
Meaning the remainder, it does come from French [[from:rester]]: it is the stuff that stays.
French for a reminder, written under repeated speed-limit signs; literally to recall, it's also English for abseiling and a doublet of [[same-root:repeal]].
A doublet of [[same-root:rappel]], from the same source.
French for injured, not blessed, though it shares a root with English [[same-root:blessed]].
Essentially means struck by God or a holy force, sharing a root with French [[same-root:blessé]], injured.
When a Southern lady says it, Jess explains, she is being very judgmental and patronizing.
French for a rental, not a place, though Rob reasons it comes from Latin [[from:locus]], place.
French for a bookshop, not a library, which is a [[see:bibliothèque]].
The French word for a library, which the hosts love; not to be confused with [[see:librairie]].
French for a recipe, so asking for one after paying gets you the recipe, not a receipt.
French for a doctor, not medicine.
Asking for a doctor, in France or in English, might get you someone with a PhD who can't help in an emergency.
French slang for penis, pronounced 'beet', so French people laugh at Irish pub signs offering 'a bite from Ireland'.
In French a pencil, not what English calls a crayon.
Danish, Swedish and Norwegian for paintbrush, basically a cognate of pencil, from a Latin word meaning tail or penis.
Named because it looks like a paintbrush, not a pencil, from the same Latin word as [[same-root:pensel]].
French for arms, pronounced like bra; English [[gave:brassiere]] comes from the French for 'arm thing'.
From the French for 'arm thing', from [[from:bras]]; a euphemism skirting what it actually covers.
In French a sports bra or unwired bra; an ordinary bra is a [[see:soutien-gorge]].
The French for a bra, another euphemism like [[see:brassiere]], literally a throat support.
Jess explains it as having a long slender neck, connecting it with the throat in [[see:soutien-gorge]].
French for bread, which Rob says is superb.
French for a corner, not money; a coin is a [[see:pièce]].
French for a coin, while a piece is a [[see:morceau]].
French for a piece or morsel.
French for mushroom, also used in English; a doublet of [[same-root:champion]], from the idea of a field, as mushrooms grow in fields.
Originally a combatant in the field, a gladiator or fighter; a doublet of [[same-root:champignon]] and possibly [[same-root?:campaign]].
Suggested by Jess as a potential third doublet of [[same-root?:champion]] and [[same-root?:champignon]].
The region may be named after fields, making it a possible fourth doublet with [[same-root?:champion]].
In English often a train or musical conductor, whereas in most European languages it means a driver.
Fiercer in English than in Romance languages, where it means to check or examine, a sense [[see:Euro English]] adopts.
English spoken among Europeans, notably in Brussels, using words like [[see:control]], [[see:actual]], [[see:realize]] and [[see:eventually]] in senses native speakers wouldn't recognise.
In Euro English it means current, as French [[see:actuel]] and German [[see:aktuell]] do, rather than real.
French for current, leading Euro English speakers to use [[see:actual]] that way.
German for current, leading Euro English speakers to use [[see:actual]] that way.
Euro English uses it to mean making something occur, as in realizing a dream, not something occurring to you.
In Euro English it means possibly, as German [[see:eventuell]] and French [[see:éventuellement]] do, not 'at some point'.
German for possibly, behind the Euro English use of [[see:eventually]].
French for possibly, behind the Euro English use of [[see:eventually]].
Negative in English but meaning worship in most European languages; from a root meaning to till or cultivate, like [[same-root:culture]].
Rob wonders if continental cult is closer to it; Jess confirms both come from a root meaning to till, like [[same-root:cult]].
German for bath, as in Danish, Dutch, Norwegian and Swedish; spa towns must meet a standard to bear it; a cognate of [[same-root:bath]], unlike [[unrelated:bad]].
Unrelated to Germanic [[unrelated:Bad (German)]]; possibly from Old English [[from?:bæddel]], a slur for effeminate men, it became standard around Middle English, Old English using [[see:evil]].
Old English words related to it served for [[see:bad]] as the opposite of good, surviving in 'good and evil'.
Rob adds that Old English also used words related to it for [[see:bad]].
A false cognate of [[unrelated:bad]] but a true cognate of German [[same-root:Bad (German)]], as English th often matches a Germanic d.
German for emergency, as in [[see:Notausgang]], not English 'not'.
German for emergency exit; someone knowing only that Ausgang means exit might read it as 'not the exit' and turn away.
German for a journey or way, from the verb [[from:fahren]], to go or drive; Jess's family joked about 'Fahrt, Germany' on exit signs.
German for almost, so a German who has done something fast hasn't done it.
Can mean tight or stuck; the speedy sense comes from sticking to an intense pace, a contronym Rob covered in a video; compare German [[see:fast (German)]].
A word in another language built from English-looking material with a meaning English speakers wouldn't recognise, like German [[see:Handy (German)]].
German for a mobile phone, artificial pseudo-English built on German Hand; many Germans allegedly think it's English.
Used in Indonesian and Korean for a mobile phone, a variation on German [[see:Handy (German)]].
Rob says English has only the adjective, then realises there is a crude noun sense, one of his worst moments on the podcast.
German for the single-strap backpack fashionable in the 1990s, funny given the English meaning of a bag for corpses.
What English shops sometimes call the bag German calls a [[see:Bodybag]].
Literally German for backpack, from Rück, back.
Jess's answer for the German term for a corpse bag, which Rob glosses as a dead body bag and prefers to [[see:Bodybag]].
Barely exists in other Germanic languages, perhaps only in a German dialect; they use words like [[see:Körper]], lich or [[see:Leib]] instead.
German for body, related to corpse, used where English says [[see:body]].
Another Germanic word for body, cited in contrast with English [[see:body]].
German for a photography or filming session, so a family portrait could sound like a mass shooting.
German for a vintage car, used blissfully unaware of the English meaning; Rob's favourite.
German pseudo-anglicism for bullying.
German for a pinball machine, with a whole park near Berlin devoted to them; Rob finds it more pertinent than [[see:pinball]].
Named because play starts by shooting the ball with the pin, though Rob thinks German [[see:Flipper]] better describes the game.
German for a projector, something that beams an image onto a wall; English speakers in Germany have adopted it.
British slang for a BMW; the French call the car a [[see:BM (French)]].
What the French call a BMW, dropping the last letter.
American slang for a bowel movement, which Rob knows from Family Guy.
In Dutch, as in Amsterdam, a shop selling cannabis rather than coffee, though coffee is usually available.
German for concise or pithy, not pregnant, from the same Latin word as English [[same-root:pregnant]].
Romanian for evident, marked or manifest, from the same Latin word as English [[same-root:pregnant]].
Swedish word that can mean pregnant but also striking or distinctive.
Dutch for poignant or meaningful.
From Latin, meaning before birth; figurative in [[see:pregnant pause]]; Old English said [[see:mid cilde]] or [[see:bearneacen]], and the 1800s [[see:poisoned]].
Uses the figurative sense of [[see:pregnant]] found in German [[see:prägnant]] and similar words.
An Old English way of saying [[equivalent:pregnant]].
Old English for pregnant, meaning child-adding or increasing with child.
In the 1800s could mean pregnant, bringing the hosts full circle to German [[see:Gift (German)]], poison.
In many European languages, a dinner jacket or tuxedo, the kind with shiny lapels.
Rob compares continental [[see:smoking]] with it, describing its shiny lapels.
Named for [[from:Tuxedo, New York]], a wealthy place near Jess.
The more formal British English term, which oddly covers the whole outfit, not just the jacket.
Reading historical novels as a child, Jess pictured a frilly nightgown, imagining Ebenezer Scrooge in one.
Spanish for to bother, as in 'no me molestes'; a German cameraman carried this sense into English [[gave:molest]].
Its English meaning ultimately comes from the bothering sense of [[from:molestar]] but has gone much further.
Spanish for having a cold: constipated in the nose rather than the bottom.
Spanish for bungee jumping, from [[from:puente]], bridge, with an English-looking -ing.
French for jogging, also found in other languages; Rob's least favourite French word because it looks English but isn't.
French for celebrities, a boomerang: English got people from French, which reborrowed it, perhaps because many celebrities are American.
French for a makeover, which Jess likes and Rob hates, disliking how French pronounces borrowed English words the French way.
A popular French TV show where women buy outfits and the others tell them how awful they look.
Italian for the joker in a deck of cards.
Italian for a spa.
German for general well-being, as in a wellness spa; Rob notes English has only lately taken to the word.
German for working from home, big during the pandemic, unlike the British [[see:Home Office]].
The British interior ministry, unlike German [[see:Homeoffice]]; the hosts guess the American counterpart is the [[see:Department of the Interior]].
Suggested as the American counterpart of the British [[see:Home Office]], in charge of police and the like.
Italian for remote work.
German for fat, a relative of English [[same-root:thick]], since English th often matches a Germanic d.
A relative of German [[same-root:dick (German)]], fat.
German for buttermilk, considered fatty milk, from [[from:dick (German)]].
In Norwegian and Swedish a plate, saucer or barrel, related to English [[same-root:vat]].
Related to the Nordic [[same-root:fat (Swedish)]], a plate or barrel.
In Albanian and Catalan, luck, chance, fate or destiny, related to [[same-root:fate]].
Related to the Albanian and Catalan [[same-root:fat (Catalan)]], luck or destiny.
Cantonese for to show or exhibit, unrelated to the other words spelled fat.
Swedish for the end of something, so you get off a bus's last stop at the [[see:slutstation]].
Swedish for the last station, from [[from:slut (Swedish)]], end.
Originally used for slovenly men before loose women, as discussed in an earlier episode; Rob recalls a Conservative MP using the word family to mean untidy.
A Malay word for a species of beetle, offered as a word that sounds dirty in English.
The Danish for dune, offered as a word that sounds rude to English speakers.
In Victorian society meant to exclaim suddenly, which makes novels awkward now that a sexual meaning has taken over.
Could just mean a building, Rob notes, though it's hard to say without seeming to mean something else.
Also means dialogue, among English words overtaken by sexual meanings.
Using super instead of very strikes Rob as very European; he picked it up after moving to Germany.
